title: When Good Sleep Suddenly Gets Worse
hook: Sleep that was going well can fall apart around growth spurts, teething, travel, or illness. These rough patches are normal, they pass, and a steady routine helps you ride them out.
key_points: Babies' sleep patterns change as they grow — expect ups and downs, not a straight line.
Growth spurts, teething, and illness can all temporarily disrupt sleep; so can travel and routine changes.
These rough patches are phases that pass; you don't need to overhaul everything.
A consistent, soothing bedtime routine — plus the usual safe-sleep basics — helps you ride them out.
content_html: If your baby was sleeping beautifully and then suddenly isn't, you haven't done anything wrong — sleep just doesn't improve in a straight line. The NHS points out that babies change their sleep patterns as they grow, and that growth spurts, teething, and illnesses can all affect how your baby sleeps. Travel and other changes to the routine can do the same.
extra_html: The reassuring part is that these rough patches are phases, and they pass. You don't usually need to overhaul your whole approach; the NHS advice is to be prepared to adapt routines as your baby enters different stages, while keeping a consistent, soothing bedtime routine as your anchor. The usual safe-sleep basics — a firm, flat, bare surface, baby on their back — stay in place throughout. This is general guidance; if your baby's sleep problems persist or you're worried, speak to your health visitor or doctor.

related.title: Toddler Sleep: Routines and Naps
related.hook: Toddlers (1–2 years) typically need 11–14 hours of sleep per 24 hours, naps included. A predictable bedtime routine does more for sleep than almost anything else.

related.title: Sleep Training, Without the Dogma
related.hook: There's no single 'right' way to help a baby sleep. Readiness is usually around 4–6 months, methods range from gradual check-ins to gentler approaches, and consistency matters most.
